Postnatal Complications

Postnatal complications — postpartum haemorrhage, infection, subinvolution, thromboembolism and postpartum psychiatric disorders.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Recognise postpartum haemorrhage and sepsis
  • Manage subinvolution and urinary problems
  • Identify thromboembolism signs
  • Screen for postnatal depression and psychosis

In simple words

The first days after birth carry risk. Haemorrhage and infection kill most quickly, and emotional problems follow soon after.

Postnatal complications

Complication Signs
Postpartum haemorrhage Heavy bleeding, soft uterus, bleeding over 500 mL
Puerperal sepsis Fever above 24 hours after birth, foul lochia, tender uterus
Endometritis Fever, lower abdominal pain, offensive discharge
Subinvolution Slow uterine descent and prolonged lochia
Urinary retention Inability to void, painful distended bladder
Mastitis and breast abscess Red painful breast, fever, cracked nipple
Thrombophlebitis or pulmonary embolism Sudden breathlessness, chest pain, calf pain
Postnatal depression Low mood, tearfulness, poor care, guilt
Postnatal psychosis Delusions, confusion, refusal to feed the baby

Nursing actions by complication

  • PPH: call for help, rub the uterus, give oxytocic, check for tears and retained products, compress the aorta, fluids and blood
  • Sepsis: cultures, antibiotics, perineal care, isolation if infectious
  • Subinvolution: treat infection and anaemia; review for retained products
  • Urinary retention: privacy, warm water, catheterise if needed
  • Mastitis: continue feeding, correct attachment, warm compress, antibiotics as prescribed
  • Thromboembolism: report breathlessness and calf pain; anticoagulants as prescribed
  • Postnatal depression: screen with EPDS, reassure, refer; protect mother and baby

🔴 Fever after delivery is never normal

Any fever after 24 hours from delivery needs urgent assessment for endometritis, wound or breast infection, urinary infection or deep vein thrombosis. Early antibiotics prevent septic shock.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Postpartum haemorrhage is the leading cause of maternal death.
  2. Puerperal sepsis shows fever, tender uterus and foul lochia.
  3. Mastitis is treated by continued breastfeeding, attachment correction and antibiotics.
  4. Postnatal depression is screened with the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale.
  5. Sudden breathlessness and chest pain suggest pulmonary embolism.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Postnatal blues are common in the first week.
  2. Postnatal psychosis is an emergency and needs psychiatric referral.
  3. Anaemia and malnutrition delay involution.
  4. Breastfeeding reduces bleeding and aids involution.
  5. Perineal care and handwashing prevent infection.

📌 Memory trick

Complications: B-I-M-P — Bleeding, Infection, Mental health, Pain or swelling.

60-second revision

  • PPH: massage, oxytocics, fluids, blood.
  • Sepsis: fever, foul lochia; cultures and antibiotics.
  • Subinvolution, urinary retention, mastitis, thromboembolism.
  • Postnatal blues, depression and psychosis need screening and referral.
  • Fever after 24 hours is never normal.

Test yourself

Fever with foul lochia after delivery suggests:

Answer: B. Fever with offensive discharge and tender uterus indicates endometritis or sepsis.

Which tool screens postnatal depression?

Answer: B. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is the standard screening tool.

Mastitis is managed by:

Answer: B. Stopping breastfeeding worsens mastitis; continue feeding with correct attachment and treat as prescribed.

Sudden breathlessness after delivery suggests:

Answer: B. Breathlessness and chest pain after birth suggest pulmonary embolism and need urgent referral.

The leading cause of maternal death is:

Answer: A. Postpartum haemorrhage is the leading direct cause of maternal death.
